title: United States v. Nixon (1974): the tapes go public
t: United States v. Nixon (1974): the tapes go public
description:
The Supreme Court's unanimous 1974 decision forced President Nixon to surrender the Watergate tapes; their transcripts became public record and ended a presidency. The case established that executive privilege cannot shield criminal evidence.

The tapes' public release remains the benchmark for unsealing: no one is above the record.

title: How unsealing works
description:
Courts seal records to protect privacy, safety, or fair trials — and unseal them when the public interest outweighs the harm. Journalists and advocates routinely move to unseal; judges weigh the First Amendment right of access against the reasons for secrecy.

The presumption in American courts favors openness: sealing is the exception.

definitions.Protective order: A court order limiting disclosure of sensitive litigation material; lifting it unseals records.
definitions.Public record: Government records open to public inspection by law.
definitions.Investigative journalism: Reporting that uncovers concealed matters of public importance — often the engine of unsealing.

source: Court records via PACER/Justia; National Archives; ICIJ publications; Congressional reports
million_march: MILLION IN PROGRESS — marching to 1,000,000 full records
